facts.statement: Boverisuchus fossils date from the Early to Middle Eocene, specifically the Ypresian to Lutetian stages.
Boverisuchus was a relatively small crocodyliform, estimated to reach 2.2 to 3.6 meters in length and weigh around 100 kilograms.
facts.quote: It was a relatively small crocodyliform with an estimated total length of approximately 2.2 - 3.6 m and a weight of around 100 kg.

facts.statement: The type species was originally described from Lutetian deposits in Germany alongside Weigeltisuchus geiseltalensis.
facts.quote: from the Lutetian of Germany alongside Weigeltisuchus geiseltalensis

facts.statement: In 2013, Brochu assigned the species formerly known as Crocodylus vorax or Pristichampsus vorax as the second species of Boverisuchus.
facts.quote: Brochu (2013) also assigned Crocodylus vorax, which has been referred to as Pristichampsus vorax since Langston (1975), as the second species of Boverisuchus.

facts.statement: Boverisuchus was reinstated as a valid genus in 2013 after Pristichampsus rollinati was deemed a nomen dubium due to insufficient diagnostic material.
facts.quote: Following a revision of the genus Pristichampsus by Brochu (2013), P. rollinati was found to be based on insufficiently diagnostic material and therefore is a nomen dubium while Boverisuchus was reinstated as a valid genus.

facts.statement: The family name Planocraniidae was reinstated to include Boverisuchus and related genera, replacing the name Pristichampsidae.
facts.quote: The name Planocraniidae was reinstated to contain these genera and replace Pristichampsidae.

facts.statement: Boverisuchus is assumed to have had heavily armored skin and long limbs adapted for a running habitus.
facts.quote: Based on other planocraniids, Boverisuchus is assumed to have had heavily armoured skin, and long limbs suggesting a cursorial (i.e. running) habitus.

facts.statement: Boverisuchus possessed hoof-like toes, suggesting it lived primarily on land and likely hunted terrestrial mammals.
facts.quote: It also had hoof-like toes, suggesting that it lived more on land than in the water, and that it therefore probably hunted terrestrial mammals.

facts.statement: Boverisuchus had ziphodont teeth that were laterally compressed, sharp, and serrated, indicating it could not drown its prey.
facts.quote: The teeth of Boverisuchus were ziphodont; i.e., laterally compressed, sharp, and with serrated edges (characteristic of terrestrial crocodyliforms that are unable to dispatch their prey by drowning them).

facts.statement: Boverisuchus teeth were initially mistaken for theropod dinosaur teeth, leading to a false belief that non-avian dinosaurs survived the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction.
facts.quote: Due to their similarity to those of certain theropod dinosaurs they were initially mistaken for theropod teeth, leading paleontologists to believe that some non-avian dinosaurs survived the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.

facts.statement: Some specimens show a tail that was round in cross-section and lacked the osteoderm crest seen in modern crocodiles, resembling a dinosaur's tail.
facts.quote: Some material referred to Pristichampsus rollinatii shows further features adapting the animal to this lifestyle. The tail was more reminiscent of a dinosaur's, being round in cross-section and lacking the osteoderm crest observed in extant crocodile species.
It would also have been capable of galloping.

facts.statement: The time range for Boverisuchus is estimated from 61.66 to 37.71 million years ago, spanning the Selandian to Bartonian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Selandian to Bartonian (61.66 to 37.71 million years ago)

facts.statement: In 2026, Lindblad et al. described the first Boverisuchus specimen from the middle-late Paleocene of Saskatchewan, Canada.
facts.quote: Lindblad et al. (2026) describe two new crocodyliform specimens from the Paleocene strata of the Ravenscrag Formation (Saskatchewan, Canada), including the first member of the genus Boverisuchus from the middle-late Paleocene of Saskatchewan

facts.statement: It is debated how to classify Planocraniidae, with a 2021 study noting a lack of consensus and difficulty in placing the group.
facts.quote: In 2021, Rio & Mannion conducted a new phylogenetic study using a heavily modified morphological data set, and also noted the lack of consensus and difficulty in placing Planocraniidae.

facts.statement: Boverisuchus belongs to the family Planocraniidae.
Boverisuchus is classified within the order Crocodilia.
Boverisuchus is classified within the suborder Eusuchia.
